---
title: "Enhanced Neuroplasticity"
author: "Anselm Jeong"
date: "2026-01-31"
bibliography: "Metaplasticity.bib"
---

The proposition that ECT-induced brain plasticity is the primary determinant of therapeutic outcome is supported by a robust and diverse body of evidence spanning multiple biological scales [@Yan2019; @Tozzi2021; @Dukart2014]. At the macroscopic level, the GEMRIC consortium mega-analysis demonstrated consistent hippocampal volume increases of approximately 2.6–5% after ECT courses, with the greatest changes observed in the dentate gyrus [@Oltedal2018; @Tendolkar2013]. These structural gains reflect a complex tapestry of underlying cellular processes, including neurogenesis, gliogenesis, synaptogenesis, and angiogenesis.

If the generalized seizure and subsequent CSD represent the physical act of "rebooting" the system, then the metabolic and molecular cascades that follow reopen a plasticity window. This period, spanning hours to days following treatment, represents a time-limited state of enhanced neural plasticity where pathological circuits become amenable to adaptive remodeling. The transition into this state is orchestrated by a coordinated neurotrophic and intracellular cascades. The primary driver is the upregulation of Brain-Derived Neurotrophic Factor (BDNF), which activates TrkB receptors and initiates downstream MAPK/ERK and PI3K/Akt signaling pathways [@Minichiello2009; @Nibuya1995].

The temporal dynamics of the BDNF changes are critical for estimating the duration of the plasticity window. In a meta-analysis of human studies, ECT significantly increases BDNF, with individual studies reporting 30–100% increases from baseline following a typical 6–12 session course [@Brunoni2014; @Rocha2016]. These elevated levels last for approximately one week before gradually returning toward baseline, indicating that the plasticity window persists well beyond the immediate post-ictal phase. Animal studies highlight the importance of repeated sessions to prolong the plasticity window. While a single ECT session produced only a transient BDNF elevation that lasted only 24–48 hours, repeated sessions progressively lengthen the duration, with sustained elevation persisting for at least two weeks [@Newton2003]. This contrast between single and repeated sessions explains the clinical observation that therapeutic response typically emerges after 4–6 sessions, which may be the point at which the plasticity window becomes sufficiently stabilized to support lasting circuit remodelling.

At the cellular level, this plasticity-enhanced environment translates into actual structural changes. Animal models revealed a rapid increase in dendritic spine density in the hippocampus and prefrontal cortex, progressing from fragile "thin" spines to stable "mushroom" configurations over 1–2 weeks [@Chen2009]. Simultaneously, epigenetic modifications, such as increased histone acetylation and TET1-mediated DNA demethylation at BDNF gene promoters, provide the necessary molecular memory to maintain the plasticity window over extended durations [@Tsankova2004; @Guo2011].
